input.question: How was the NASA mission Magellan able to map the Venusian surface so quickly?
input.ground_truth: Venus’ day is 243 earth days long. Magellan orbited Venus every 3 hours or so. That means that during a single Venusian day, the probe circled the planet almost 2000 times. I don’t know what you mean by quickly, but it took almost an entire earth year to get that 96%, for what it’s worth.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How was the NASA mission Magellan able to map the Venusian surface so quickly?

Answer:

response.prediction: Okay! Imagine you want to see what’s under a big, thick blanket on your bed. You can’t just lift the blanket and look, because it’s too hot and too thick. But you have a special flashlight and a camera. You turn on the flashlight and shine it through tiny holes in the blanket. The light bounces off the bed (which is like the surface of Venus) and comes back to your camera. Your camera takes lots and lots of pictures very fast, and a computer helps put all those pictures together to make a map of what’s under the blanket. That’s how the NASA Magellan mission made a map of Venus quickly—it used radar (like a special flashlight) to “see” through the thick clouds and made a map from above!
